Stealth technology in U.S. military aviation was developed primarily from the early 1950s to 1970.
Radar Cross Section (RCS) varies wildly with aspect angle due to interference effects between different parts of the aircraft.
Radar signal strength returning from a target decreases with the fourth power of the target range.
A 95% reduction in radar signature reduces radar detection range by 50%.
Dynamic RCS measurements require instrumented aircraft and precise knowledge of aspect angles, making them difficult and costly.
Model measurement of RCS uses scaled aircraft models and scaled radar wavelengths to simulate full-scale radar echoes.
Early computational methods for RCS prediction were insufficient to model complex aircraft shapes.
Radar-absorbent materials (RAM) were developed starting in 1955 to reduce radar reflections from aircraft surfaces.
RAM must be thin, lightweight, durable, and able to withstand environmental stresses without compromising aircraft aerodynamics.
Impulse measurement systems were developed to rapidly characterize the electrical properties of RAM ingredients over a wide frequency range.
The T-33 aircraft was coated with broadband RAM and successfully flown to demonstrate radar signature reduction.
Flare spots are localized radar reflection sources on aircraft that significantly contribute to RCS.
Metal screens with fine mesh can act like solid metal to radar, affecting radar signature.
The radar echo pattern of an aircraft is highly dependent on radar frequency and polarization.
Blending with the radar background is more challenging for airborne vehicles due to near-zero radar background compared to ground vehicles.
The Avionics Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base developed a large anechoic chamber known as 'the barn' for RCS measurements.
Early RCS test models were made of fiberglass over wooden frames and coated with conductive metallic paint.
The development of stealth technology was constrained by security considerations limiting public disclosure.
Radar signature reduction requires balancing cost-effectiveness against achievable signature reduction.
The paper emphasizes that stealth involves minimizing all observables, including infrared, visible, and acoustic signatures, but focuses on radar.
